title: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
subtitle: The basic accounting equation and why it always holds
openingQuestion: A company borrows 500 million to buy machinery. How does the balance sheet change?
openingOptions: Assets increase by 500 million dong, and equity also increases by exactly 500 million dong
There is no change at all on the company's balance sheet
Only the company's assets increase, with no other line item changing
explanation: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, and this equation always balances because it's simply two views of the same pool of assets: what the business has, and who has a claim on it. Every transaction touches at least two spots to keep the balance - borrowing money to buy a machine makes both assets and liabilities rise together. This underlies double-entry bookkeeping, and it's also why a balance sheet off by even one dong signals an error somewhere.

realWorldExample.description: Independent auditors always check first whether Assets = Liabilities + Equity balances before digging into individual line items - this is the most basic integrity check for any set of financial statements.

quiz.question: If a company has Assets = 1,000 million, Liabilities = 400 million, what is equity?
options: 600 million
1,000 million
400 million
1,400 million
quiz.explanation: Equity = Assets - Liabilities = 1,000 - 400 = 600 million. This is what's left for the owners.

quiz.question: The balance sheet always balances because:
options: The company's accounting staff always work with great focus and care, avoiding errors
The formula Assets = Liabilities + Equity always holds under the double-entry bookkeeping principle
This is simply a mandatory requirement under current law
In practice there is never any error whatsoever in the accounting records
quiz.explanation: The balance sheet is an expression of the base formula. Every transaction is recorded from two sides (debit-credit), so the sheet always balances - if it doesn't, there's an error.

quiz.question: A company successfully cuts costs and profit rises by 50 million. Which side of the balance sheet gets affected?
options: The Equity side rises through retained earnings
Only the Liabilities side of the balance sheet is affected by this
Only the Assets side of the balance sheet is affected by this
All three sides - assets, liabilities and equity - are affected equally
quiz.explanation: Profit → Retained Earnings → Equity rises. At the same time, cash (an asset) also rises because expenses fell. The balance still holds.

quiz.question: Why does profit that just appeared on the income statement affect equity on the balance sheet?
options: It has no effect whatsoever on the company's equity on the balance sheet
Because these two financial statements are, by their nature, entirely unrelated to each other
Because the accounting department double-counted the same profit figure on two different reports
Because profit accumulates into 'Retained Earnings' on the balance sheet
quiz.explanation: The three statements connect: income statement → Retained Earnings → balance sheet. Profit from the income statement is added to Retained Earnings, a component of equity.

quiz.question: Company X's equity rose from 1,000 million to 1,200 million over the year. This increase could be due to:
options: Profit or added contributed capital, minus dividends paid and share buybacks
The sole possible cause is the profit the company earned during that year
The sole possible cause is the company's liabilities rising during the year
The sole possible cause is the company having sold off part of its assets
quiz.explanation: The formula: Ending Equity = Beginning Equity + Profit + New Contributed Capital - Dividends - Share Buybacks.

quiz.question: A company IPOs and sells 1,000 shares at 10 million/share. By how much does equity rise?
options: Unchanged, since it's just a share sale
10 billion (1,000 × 10 million)
10 million (the price of one share)
1 billion (1,000 × 1 million)
quiz.explanation: Selling shares = receiving new capital = assets (cash) rise = equity rises by 10 billion. The company receives cash from new share investors.

quiz.question: Is a high ROE (say, 30%) always good?
options: Always good, because a high ROE means the company is efficient
Cannot be judged without knowing the share price
Not certain - it could be driven by debt leverage shrinking equity
Always bad, since a high ROE usually carries a lot of risk
quiz.explanation: A high ROE can come from two different sources: business efficiency or high financial leverage. It needs to be viewed alongside the D/E ratio, ROA, and earnings quality.

keyTakeaways: Every transaction touches at least two lines on the balance sheet
This is the foundation of double-entry bookkeeping

practicePrompt.question: A company just borrowed an additional 300 million in cash from a bank to expand its warehouse. Right after this transaction, how do the two sides of the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity change?
options: Both sides rise by 300 million: assets go up, liabilities go up by the same amount, and it still balances
Only the Assets side rises by 300 million, while Liabilities and Equity remain completely unchanged
Only the Liabilities side rises by 300 million, while the company's Assets don't change at all
Equity will rise by 300 million because this is new cash the company received to use
practicePrompt.explanation: Borrowing money is a transaction that acts on two sides at once: cash (an asset) rises by 300 million, and the obligation to repay the bank (a liability) also rises by exactly 300 million - this is a textbook example of double-entry bookkeeping, and the accounting equation automatically balances after every transaction.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Every transaction touches at least two lines on the balance sheet

application.title: Test the accounting equation with a transaction
application.message: Think up a hypothetical transaction (borrowing 50 million to buy a motorbike for a delivery service) and write out how it affects Assets and Liabilities, then check whether the equation still balances.
application.secondary: If the two sides don't match, you've missed one effect of the transaction.

sections.text: Before reading any detailed figure on a set of financial statements, an auditor always checks one thing first: does Assets equal Liabilities plus Equity. If it doesn't balance, the entire report has a serious problem.

Assets = Liabilities + Equity is the most foundational equation of the entire accounting system. It reflects a simple truth: every asset a business holds is financed from one of two sources - either borrowed (liabilities), or contributed by shareholders/accumulated profit (equity). No asset 'falls from the sky' without a corresponding funding source.
Every transaction affects at least two line items

Because the equation must always balance, every economic transaction must simultaneously affect at least two positions in the equation. **Example:** a company borrows 500 million dong from a bank to buy machinery - assets rise by 500 million (new machinery), while liabilities also rise by 500 million (the bank loan). Both sides rise together, and the equation stays balanced.

Another example: a company records 200 million dong of net profit in the period. Assets rise by 200 million (more cash or receivables), while equity also rises by 200 million (retained earnings up). The company's business results are always directly 'wired' into the balance sheet through the retained-earnings channel.

items: Borrowing to buy inventory → Assets rise, Liabilities rise by the same amount
Shareholders contribute more capital in cash → Assets (cash) rise, Equity rises by the same amount
Paying a supplier in cash → Assets (cash) fall, Liabilities fall by the same amount
Recording net profit for the period → Assets rise, Equity (retained earnings) rises by the same amount

concepts.def: Assets = Liabilities + Equity - always holds for every business, at every point in time.
The system of recording every transaction into at least two accounts to keep the equation balanced.
The only two sources funding assets: liabilities or equity.

sections.label: Why this is the first thing an auditor checks
sections.text: If Assets ≠ Liabilities + Equity, there is certainly a missing entry, a duplicated entry, or an error/fraud in the books - because the mathematical nature of double entry doesn't allow an imbalance if the process is followed correctly. This is the most basic integrity check before digging into any individual line item.

lines: Assets = Liabilities + Equity isn't an optional rule - it is the very definition of the balance sheet.
Understanding this equation lets you self-check the logic of any financial transaction you encounter.
